balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Tesla, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Tesla, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Tesla, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Tesla, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Tesla, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Tesla, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Tesla, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Tesla, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Tesla, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

automotiveMargin.title: Automotive gross margin: reported vs ex-credits
automotiveMargin.content:
Automotive gross margin is as reported; ex-credits strips out the sale of ZEV/GHG regulatory credits to other automakers, a high-margin revenue line tied to emissions rules rather than vehicle economics.

For Tesla, Inc.: the spread between the two lines is the gap competitors cannot copy by cutting price -- it is pure policy upside, and it narrows as rivals build their own EVs and need fewer purchased credits.

What to watch:

  • Ex-credits margin trend in isolation -- the business the DCF actually prices
  • Widening spread signalling rising reliance on credit sales
  • Regulatory rollback risk (the 2026 US EPA/CAFE changes cut this pool further)

regulatoryCredits.title: Regulatory credit revenue
regulatoryCredits.content:
Regulatory credit revenue is cash Tesla collects from other automakers buying ZEV/GHG compliance credits it generates by selling zero-emission vehicles. It is close to pure profit (near-zero cost of sale) and entirely outside Tesla's control -- a political and regulatory input, not a product one.

For Tesla, Inc.: this line has been shrinking as the credit pool tightens and peers electrify; it is explicitly excluded from the DCF's owner FCF build precisely because it is not a repeatable operating cash flow.

What to watch:

  • Quarter-over-quarter decline as the regulatory tailwind fades
  • Automotive margin excluding this line (see the chart above) as the better read of the core business

energyMargin.title: Energy generation & storage gross margin
energyMargin.content:
Energy gross margin covers Megapack/Powerwall storage and solar -- the smaller, faster-growing segment next to automotive.

For Tesla, Inc.: this margin has run above automotive's in recent quarters, so segment mix shift toward energy is a margin tailwind the blended GrossMargin line does not isolate.

What to watch:

  • Margin trend as Megapack factory utilisation scales
  • Lumpiness from project-based storage deployment timing

energyStorageDeployed.title: Energy storage deployed
energyStorageDeployed.content:
Storage deployed is Megapack and Powerwall capacity installed in the period, in gigawatt-hours -- the volume driver behind energy segment revenue, independent of price or mix.

For Tesla, Inc.: this is the closest thing Tesla discloses to a unit count for its second-largest growth segment; only 13 of the CSV's periods have a value, so short runs of flat or declining GWh are as likely to be lumpy project timing as a genuine slowdown.

What to watch:

  • Sequential growth versus Megapack factory capacity additions
  • Whether storage revenue (chart above) is growing faster or slower than deployed GWh (price/mix effect)

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Tesla, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

dcf.base_sublabel: Owner FCF — after SBC, interest income & leases
dcf.model_approach_note: The sanity check flagged the first build (9.5% WACC) for an implied P/E of 417.9x against a 10-year average of 179.3x. Most of that gap is a denominator effect -- SBC-adjusted trailing EPS is a few tens of cents on a 3.3% operating margin, so almost any positive franchise value reads as an extreme multiple -- but part of it was a real model gap: a 9.5% rate built on a 1.05 beta priced an average-risk equity, not a business whose operating income has fallen roughly 4x in three years and whose recovery leans on a regulatory approval (unsupervised autonomy) it does not control. The one-shot fix adds +1.0% for that cyclicality and +1.0% for the regulatory single-point-of-failure risk, taking WACC to 11.5% across all three scenarios -- growth, margins, capex and probability weights were left unchanged. That moves weighted intrinsic value from $158.09 to $111.49 (bear $16.42 / base $81.46 / bull $266.62) against a market price near $390: even the bull case, at the risk-adjusted discount rate, sits roughly a third below where the stock trades. Investment framing: today's price is a bet that the bull path (robotaxi, FSD licensing, Optimus) lands close to certainty, discounted at a rate below what the cyclical core business and its regulatory dependence call for -- this model does not say that optionality is worthless, only that an owner paying today's price is underwriting the bull case plus a sub-10% WACC.
